ORA: Open Robot‑Use Agents

An open robot-use harness that connects open-weight language models to robots.

October 2026 · 22 min · Yuanbo Yang, Siyi Chen, Jun Gao, Hao Zhang

Yuanbo Yang, Siyi Chen, Jun Gao, Hao Zhang

October 2026

CodeAppendixGallery · 153 episodes

TL;DR: ORA is an open robot-use agent harness that lets open-weight language models operate robots fully zero-shot: no VLA, no robot training and no task-specific memory, with results on RoboTwin and LIBERO-Pro (69.2% and 81.4% by the official success checks) competitive with agents built on frontier models. It gets there with a harness designed for robot tasks in the physical world: exact task and environment context, tools for perception and motion, and context management.

ORA harness (ours) + open-weight model, zero-shotRPent agent harness + language model + VLA + task-specific memoryVLA policies and other methods

Figure 2. Success rates on (a) RoboTwin C2R (250 cases) and (b) LIBERO-Pro (800 cases), using the same case lists as RPent[1]. ORA runs every case zero-shot, with no demonstrations or task-specific memory. Baseline rates come from RPent's leaderboard. [a] Astra uses frozen memory batches. [b] Flash Mode uses released memory and reports the best of ten seeds. Full protocol and values: appendix.

Evaluation cases and baseline models

RoboTwin C2R (clean-to-randomized) covers 50 tasks with 5 seeds each in randomized scenes. LIBERO-Pro covers eight Task and Swap suites with 10 tasks and 10 seeds each. ORA rates count every case.

RPent combines a language model, VLA and task-specific memory collected in an earlier exploration pass. Models include GPT-5.5, Opus-4.7, GPT-6 Astra and open-weight Qwen3.6-27B[2]. End-to-end VLA baselines are π0.5[3], π_RLinf[4], GR00T-N1.7[5], LingBot-VLA[6] and AtomVLA[7]. RPent Flash Mode uses Molmo2-8B[8] with released memory.

These are comparisons of complete systems with different tools, memory and protocols. Rates use official success checks, which can overstate task completion; see Limitations.

Introduction

ORA is an open robot-use agent harness that enables open-weight models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash[9] to solve robot tasks (Figure 3). It leads agents built on closed frontier models on RoboTwin and comes close to them on LIBERO-Pro (Figure 2). Below we explain why robot use needs agents driven by open models and where ORA sits among existing methods.

Why robot-use agents

LLM agents now handle much digital work, including coding[11] and computer use, as computer-use agents (CUAs)[12][13]. However, most existing robot policies, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs)[14][15] and world action models (WAMs)[16], still rely on robot-specific training data, collected by teleoperation[17], with handheld grippers such as UMI[18] or from egocentric videos[19]. An alternative is to build on the reasoning and tool calling of existing LLM agents. As a recent talk asked: could a strong enough agent operate a robot from its manual alone (Figure 4)[20]?

This suggests bringing the agent loop to the physical world, as in a recent robot-use agent[22]: a tool call moves the robot, the model reasons about what it sees, and the next camera frame starts the next turn. Meanwhile, frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra have shown strong zero-shot direct robot control (Figure 5)[21], and several recent demos operate robots this way[23][24][25].

Open-weight models, however, have barely been tested on this, yet robot use needs them for two reasons. First, to understand how well language models manipulate objects and how to improve them, we need large amounts of reproducible data, which means a model we can serve ourselves and experiment with at an acceptable cost, rather than paying frontier-model API prices. Second, a deployed robot system built on an LLM must be fast and efficient enough to run on local hardware. That needs an open model small enough to deploy, and task data that only an open model makes affordable to collect.

Where ORA fits

Methods that control robots with learned models fall into four families. They differ in the role of the language model and in how often it makes a decision (Table 1).

Vision-language-action (VLA) models[14][3][15] and, more recently, world action models that also predict future video[16][26] map camera images and an instruction to actions at every control step and are trained on the largest robot datasets. Because the vision-language backbone is fine-tuned into a visuomotor policy that outputs actions, these systems use little of its ability to reason and act as an agent, for example to measure before moving, plan several steps ahead or change approach after a failure.

A common response is to add a language model as a planner on top of a learned policy, the System 2 / System 1 design[27][28][29][5]. The language model splits the task into steps and the policy carries them out. In RPent[1], a language model directs a VLA policy using task-specific memory. The model can also command some motions itself, but most of the manipulation is still done by the VLA, which is trained on robot demonstrations.

A third family has the language model write the policy as code. Code as Policies[30] turns the scene and the task into a program that calls perception and control primitives. CaP-Agent0[31], ASPIRE[32] and RATs[33] add an agent that runs the program, reads the outcome and revises it; ASPIRE and RATs also keep the skills that work. These methods need no robot demonstrations, and they are economical to run: the model is called once or a few times per task, and the program then runs without it. The price is that the program executes as one or a few open-loop segments. Getting it right often takes trial runs (ASPIRE, for example, learns its skills on separate seeds before it is tested), and between revisions no model looks at the scene: the program reacts only through the checks written into it, which limits how well it carries over to new scenes.

The fourth family runs the agent loop directly, in the ReAct style[34]: the model reasons, calls a tool, reads the result and decides again. Frontier models have controlled robots this way[21][23], and Guava[35], OpenRUA[36], Agent as Policy[37] and Robo-Harness K1[38] are harnesses for such agents. When the model issued every low-level command itself, the best model in one study reached 5.5% on LIBERO[23]. ORA is in this family. Each tool call covers one bounded motion, which a controller executes, and the model sees the result before its next decision. It costs a model call at every step, so at today's latencies and prices this family is slower and costlier to run than a program written once (see Cost and Limitations).

How ORA works

ORA follows the practice of coding agents such as Claude Code[39] and Pi[40]: the task runs as a ReAct loop[34] in which, every turn, the model reads its input, thinks and makes one tool call; the action changes the state of the world, and what comes back becomes the next turn's input (Figure 6). Like those agents, it has a prompt bundle, tools and context management, but for a robot each has to do more.

First, the prompt bundle has to describe the body of each embodiment and the task: the robot's frames, the point each command moves, the gripper's constants, and the task's success criteria written out in detail. Second, the tool suite has to help the model sense and act in the physical environment. In place of a shell and file reads and writes, the model sees the world only through cameras and the robot's sensors, so it needs perception tools that measure the real scene and action tools that act on the environment and report, after every action, exactly what happened. Third, compared with a coding agent, a robot-use agent receives a large volume of redundant visual observations and environment data, so context management has to carry much heavier input: every turn adds camera images, and the model keeps returning to earlier results. The input must stay small without losing those results or breaking the prompt cache.

On the other side is the environment: a supervisor checks every motion against the robot's limits, runs it and returns a measured receipt. Throughout, the model perceives the scene only through RGB and depth images and never sees privileged information from the simulator: the success check's code, object ground truth or simulator contacts.

Environment and observation

We run ORA on three simulated benchmarks, each with its own robot (Figure 7). They differ in the simulator and its world frame, the arms, the point each command moves, the gripper's geometry, the cameras and how success is judged. RoboDojo[10] runs on Isaac Sim[41] with a two-arm ARX X5; RoboTwin[42] runs on SAPIEN[43] with a two-arm ALOHA; LIBERO[44] and LIBERO-Pro[45] run on MuJoCo[46] through robosuite[47] with a one-arm Franka.

The loop, the kinds of tools and the model are shared; only the controllers are fitted to each robot. What differs reaches the model as text, through a benchmark boundary and a robot card. With these, one model runs all three robots. The card and the boundary give the agent the details of the body and the scene it needs to reason with, such as the point each command moves, where the fingers touch and how wide the jaws open; open a card below for them.

After every action, the environment returns an observation (Figure 8). It holds an RGB image from each camera with its calibration, the measured pose and gripper of each arm, the receipt of the last action and the remaining budget, and it is paired with the observation the action was chosen from, so the model can compare before and after. Each camera's depth image is stored with the observation, and the looking tools read it when the model measures.

Prompt Bundle

A coding agent reads the repository and its instructions before it edits anything; a robot-use agent likewise has to be told enough about its environment before it moves. We therefore give it a prompt bundle of seven layers (Figure 6). A new embodiment therefore needs no training: only the embodiment context is replaced. Open any layer to read it as the model did in the run of Figure 3.

  1. System policy, the same for every robot and task: the turn protocol (read-only calls may be batched; a call that changes the world stands alone), every derived number goes to compute, how older evidence is replaced by references, and what the budgets mean.

    System message, Native Robot Policy v4, excerpt

    Turn protocol

Read-only tools may be called sequentially or in one independent batch. A
world-mutating tool must be the only tool call in its assistant response. Each
accepted mutation ends the current turn; wait for the next actual observation
before choosing another mutation.

Arithmetic belongs in the advertised calculation capability, not in your own
working. Whenever a number would be derived -- a residual, an offset along a
direction, a quaternion unpacked, a sum of extents, a dot or cross product, a
projection between image and world, a trigonometric value -- that derivation is
part of how the action was chosen […]

How this context reaches you

Current actual evidence arrives complete on every turn. Earlier evidence is not
guaranteed to stay in the form you first received it.

A result that exceeds its inline budget is replaced by a status record carrying
an exact reference to the complete original. […] Open the reference when you
need what a past result said; call again when you need what is true now.

What the reported allowances mean

Every turn reports what remains of the current session round […]: accepted world
mutations, model turns including read-only ones, and elapsed wall-clock seconds.
[…] keep enough in hand to witness the effect of your final mutation and to take
the advertised closing step: an unverified last action and an unclosed episode
are both worse than one attempt fewer.

    Verbatim from the prompt; […] marks a cut.

  2. Evidence rules, also shared: keep direct evidence, inferences, candidates, executed commands and verified effects apart; after a failure, change what the next attempt rests on.

    Evidence-to-Action Invariants v5, excerpt

    Keep these states distinct:

- **Direct evidence:** present in a current image, measurement or tool result.
- **Inferred:** a task-relevant interpretation supported by observations.
- **Candidate:** a proposed point, pose or action that has not executed.
- **Executed:** a command the Runtime accepted and attempted.
- **Verified:** a physical effect confirmed by a later observation.
[…]
When something fails

A refusal, an error or an unchanged world is evidence about the approach, not
only about the tool. Before repeating anything, change what the attempt rests
on: refresh the evidence its arguments came from, or take a different route to
the same effect. An identical call against an unchanged premise is not a
recovery, and when two attempts fail the same way the premise is what to test.

    Verbatim from the prompt; […] marks a cut.

The bundle says how to look and move. It never contains a solution, object coordinates or the success test. Three of its layers are specific to a robot task: the robot card, the task instruction copied unchanged from the benchmark, and the completion contract. See the Analysis for the role of these components.

Tool Suite

Each tool covers something the model cannot do reliably on its own (Figure 9). The model sees only what the tools measure.

A language model can name what it sees but cannot point at it precisely, the reference gap DeepSeek describes[48]. The looking tools narrow it: vision_ground and vision_segment return SAM 3[49] masks for a named object or a few pointed pixels, mark_point measures single pixels, and each is looked up in depth, so the model gets positions in metres (Figure 10).

Figure 10. Four tool calls on LIBERO-Pro, RoboDojo and RoboTwin, each with the image it returned to the model and the numbers that came back. Click a tool in Figure 6 for more calls from the run of Figure 3.

The model also does geometry in its reasoning, sometimes wrongly: 12.2% of 35,270 responses derived vectors or rotations by hand, and three runs pointed the gripper up when they meant to approach from above. compute takes that arithmetic over, and a pose can be given as directions, such as approach straight down.

Motion tools take a target for the controlled point, never joints. The environment solves inverse kinematics and plans the path with cuRobo[50], runs it and returns a receipt; a refusal says why, for instance that the straight path is reachable for only 75% of the way. grasp_plan proposes grasps with Contact-GraspNet[51], and grasp_execute runs one as a single supervised sequence.

check_task returns the official yes or no, finish_episode ends a round early when a mistake cannot be undone, and report_issue lets the model flag a fault in the harness rather than in its own attempt.

See the Analysis for the role of these components.

Context Management

A coding agent's turn adds a few lines of text; a robot's turn adds three camera images, measured poses and a receipt. Context management has to balance three goals that pull against each other. The input must stay short. Every earlier result must stay recoverable exactly, because the model often needs a number from many turns back: when we cut each observation to about half its length, rounding numbers and dropping limits, RoboDojo success fell from 17 to 10 of 27 rounds. And the start of the input must stay stable, so that the server's prompt cache keeps hitting, while every reduction breaks it.

ORA keeps the input in four layers, newest first (Figure 6). Open any layer to see it as the model received it.

    From the run's own records; … marks a cut.

To see the three goals at work, Figure 11 follows one long session: the RoboDojo block-stacking task of Figure 3, played three times in a row on the same scene, 123 turns in all.

The input stays short. In round 1 the input grew from 33k to 162k tokens, and at turns 14 and 18 the images of older steps became references. Round 2 began with round 1 still word for word; at 180k tokens, before turn 31, the model folded round 1 into a checkpoint, with its official result, a summary of facts, constraints, failed attempts and what not to repeat, and a reference to the 228 KB transcript. The input fell to 59k. Only completed rounds are folded, so round 2, which ran 65 turns, grew to 253k tokens with its older images turned into references nine times; it was folded the same way before turn 96, from 261k to 58k, and round 3 finished in 33 turns.

Nothing is lost. Every image or result that leaves the input becomes a reference to the exact stored bytes, which observe or artifact_read reopens. In the 250 RoboTwin cases, the model reopened earlier evidence 65 times, in 30 cases. In one, its left gripper had just clamped one handle of a pot; to plan the right handle, it read back the full grasp_plan result whose inline preview had been cut, 7,965 bytes of JSON, page by page.

The prefix stays stable. Between reductions, each request extends the previous one byte for byte, so the server can reuse its cache. In this session, 104 of the 122 later requests extended the previous one; the other 18 followed a reduction or opened a round, and they account for 82% of the uncached input. The estimated cache hit rate over the session was 86%, as in the evaluation runs (see Cost).

LIBERO-Pro

LIBERO-Pro[45] changes the task (Task suites) or moves the objects (Swap suites). ORA loses only two points against LIBERO and solves about as many Swap cases as Task cases (331 and 320 of 400), while VLA policies trained on LIBERO drop sharply: π_RLinf falls from 95.3% to 50.0% and AtomVLA from 97.0% to 6.3% (Table 5). On the six suites that agents writing robot code report, ORA averages 89.2%, against 71.7% for ASPIRE[32], 43.8% for RATs[33] and 18.2% for CaP-Agent0[31], under different protocols. OpenRUA[36] reports 87.0% with Claude Opus 5; we have not compared its protocol with ours.

RoboDojo: a first scan

RoboDojo[10] is the hardest: 42 multi-stage tasks on a two-arm ARX X5. A first run with an earlier version of ORA, three rounds per task, solved 18 of 126 rounds and 9 of the 42 tasks at least once. Most of the 108 failed rounds failed in motion: the target was reasonable, but the motion did not achieve it (Table 6). This is not an evaluation, and we know of no published results on this task set.

Preliminary results on a real robot

Everything above runs in simulation. We also connected ORA to a low-cost arm on a table, with a fixed RGB-D camera and a camera on the wrist, and gave DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash two household tasks: pull a small drawer open by its knob (Figure 12), and put a candy bar into a small open box (Figure 13). The loop is the one in simulation: the model reads the camera views and depth, plans each motion and reads what came back. An operator reviewed each motion before it ran. Both tasks were completed in these runs. We have not yet measured success rates.

Cost

We price every model call at DeepSeek's published off-peak rates for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash[53]: $0.003 per million cached input tokens, $0.15 per million uncached input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens. Off-peak prices are half the peak ones, so at peak rates every figure below doubles. We serve the model ourselves, so these are API-equivalent costs rather than what we paid. Every attempt counts, failures included; simulator and GPU costs are excluded.

Table 7. API-equivalent model cost of the evaluation runs reported above, at DeepSeek's off-peak USD rates for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. LIBERO counts 400 scored cases and 5 attempts that ended in an infrastructure failure and were rerun. The RoboDojo row counts the 126 rounds of the first RoboDojo run in Results (42 tasks, three rounds each, an earlier harness version), which is not an evaluation.

Most of the cost is uncached input: on LIBERO-Pro, $157 of $227, against $54 for output and $17 for cached input. Costs are also skewed. The median attempt costs well under half the mean, because long failing attempts keep adding input; a solved attempt costs $0.11 to $0.14 on average, and the 40 solved rounds in Figure 1 cost $0.13 each. An attempt produces about 100k output tokens.

Our server does not report prompt-cache hits, so we reconstruct them from token counts. A call whose input contains the whole previous request and response extends it, and that prefix counts as a hit; any other call breaks the prefix, and only the fixed prompt at its start counts. 86–89% of calls extend the previous one, which gives the estimated hit rates of 84–86% in the table. The remaining calls follow a context reduction or open a new round, and they produce 83–89% of all uncached tokens. Since uncached input is the largest cost, the main way to cut cost is to break the prefix less often.

Analysis: what the harness contributes

Earlier we argued that a robot needs more from the harness than a coding agent does. Each part came out of audits of failed runs; here we compare run versions and examine individual cases. Most comparisons do not isolate one component. Every video plays all of its panes at the same simulated-time speed, and each takeaway states its evidence and its limits.

Learning from experience

Context management keeps a finished round in the input, word for word at first and then as a checkpoint. ORA keeps no memory from one task to the next, and the benchmark runs above use one round per case, but within one session the model can draw on its earlier rounds. In Figure 14, each second round opens by stating what went wrong in the first and then avoids it; in the top row, the run of Figure 3, round 1 lost the blue block when the arm moved sideways after releasing it, and round 2 began by stating the rule to lift straight up first.

Takeaway: in the examples above, the model uses retained context to revise its approach. Across 148 two-round development sessions, round 2 succeeded in 72 and round 1 in 63. This comparison does not isolate the effect of retained context from the benefit of another attempt.

Exact task instructions and success criteria matter

The prompt bundle states the task in two parts: the benchmark's instruction, unchanged, and a completion contract that restates the official success test in plain words. When an early run set paraphrased one LIBERO-Spatial task, writing “the top layer of the wooden cabinet” for “the top drawer”, the model took the bowl standing on the cabinet instead of the one in the drawer (Figure 15). An instruction can also leave out part of the test: RoboTwin's “hold the bottle head up” also requires carrying the bottle toward the side its base pointed to, and “move the playing card away from the near edge” requires the card to end far to the left or right. Without the contract, the model satisfied the words and failed the check (Figure 16).

Takeaway: the run version using the benchmark's own words succeeded on 10 of 10 seeds, versus 2 of 10 for the version using a paraphrase. On 206 paired RoboTwin cases, the version with the completion contract succeeded on 64.1%, versus 53.4% without it. Other harness components also changed, so neither comparison isolates the effect of wording or the contract.

Perception tools help find and locate objects

The looking tools turn the model's naming and pointing into masks with measured positions and sizes (Figure 10). Early runs show why the model needs them. Its own points are not precise enough: in one LIBERO run, points chosen on the angled camera landed on the supporting surface instead of the object, and moving a point 7 to 14 pixels merged the can with the table in the mask; the size of the returned mask made the error visible. Its choice among look-alike objects is not reliable either: when text grounding ranked the wrong can first, enlarged close-ups of each candidate let the model pick the right one. Later runs repeat the second pattern (Figure 17).

Takeaway: from single early runs and with no matched ablation yet, the tools make pointing and identity errors visible, while choosing the right object stays the hardest step.

Exact constants and measurements

The tool suite gives the model measurements instead of its own estimates, and the measurement has to be the one the action needs. For placement, the tools first returned the centre of the target's mask as LIBERO's angled camera sees it, 2–3 cm from the object's centre on the table and about the whole placement tolerance. They now return the centre as seen from above (Figure 18). More generally, giving the model exact coordinates and the environment's constants, in tool results and in the system prompt, matters a great deal for its reasoning. Astranomy finds the same for GPT-6 Astra: as a direct robot policy, its success rose from 19.3% to 72.7% when the prompt added camera and gripper geometry[54].

Takeaway: returning the centre seen from above raised success on the two affected task families from 29 to 42 of 59 test states.

Explaining refused motions helps recovery

Motion tools report back after every action, and a refusal says why. Early on, when the planner found no inverse-kinematics solution and the refusal gave no reason, RoboDojo runs abandoned the target as unreachable, although most such targets were reachable with the gripper tilted; a bare error message once led a GPT-6 Astra run to repeat the same call 14 times in five minutes. A refusal now reports how far along the straight path the arm can reach and the nearest reachable orientation. In the run of Figure 3, turn 6 was refused this way, with 75% of the path reachable and a 15° tilt as the nearest reachable orientation; the model moved the build spot to where both arms could reach, and after one more refused move with the left arm it grasped the blue block with the right arm (Figure 11). Figure 19 shows two more runs: in RoboTwin, the reported reach made the model set the block down and relay it with the other arm; in LIBERO-Pro, the model took the reachable orientation the refusal offered.

Takeaway: replayed offline over 77 refused moves, a refusal that names the nearest reachable orientation resolves 69.

The gallery shows 153 solved episodes, one per task, each checked by eye.

Limitations

ORA shows that an open-weight model can operate robots zero-shot, but it has clear limits. First, it is slow: a median episode takes 14 to 25 minutes, most of it spent waiting for the model, and the simulator pauses while the model thinks, so these results say nothing about real-time control. Long-horizon tasks remain hard: the Long suites succeed 52–64% of the time, and the first RoboDojo scan solved 18 of 126 rounds. Second, the tool suite is written by hand, and ORA cannot yet iterate on or revise its tools automatically. Almost all of our results come from simulation and from one model, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash; on the real robot we have only two demonstrations, with an operator approving each motion. Our success rates use each benchmark's official check, which ends the episode the moment its condition holds, and some conditions are looser than the instruction: RoboTwin's shake tasks only check that the bottle is raised. When we watched one solved RoboTwin episode per task, 7 of 46 did not do what the instruction asks, so the reported rates overstate real task completion. This task-selected sample cannot establish a corrected overall success rate. Most of our findings come from reading failed runs, not from controlled ablations. Next, we will run ORA on more real robots and turn verified episodes into training data for a smaller model that runs on the robot.
